entry.title: March Madness Tournament Predictor
entry.content:
Heart Versus Algorithm: An Analytical Approach to Filling out my March Madness Bracket

Eric Rumsfeld
May 1st, 2026

For the 2026 NCAA D1’s Men’s Tournament, also known as March Madness, I built two brackets: one from instinct, and one from a machine learning (ML) model. Only one of them finished in the 99.4th percentile.

One Bracket from the Heart

March 15th, 2026.

Heading into Selection Sunday for this year’s March Madness Tournament, I had already decided who my champion was going to be. The Arizona Wildcats. I knew they were a team with a plan, and a team who was going to execute that plan relentlessly until they saw their colors streaming down as confetti in April. I was confident that I could pick the winner of the tournament based on vibes because I had done it previously with Baylor in 2021, UConn in 2024, and Florida in 2025. By tournament time, the Wildcats just went on a hot streak, winning some important games against Top-25-ish ranked teams like BYU, Houston, Kansas, Iowa State, as well as the Big 12 Tournament Championship. I knew they had momentum, and they knew their own strengths better than any other team. After Selection Sunday, I crafted my bracket with picks from the heart, and labeled it, ironically:

  Eric’s Golden Mean.

And One Bracket from a Forest

March 18th, 2026.

I built an ML algorithm called a random forest to predict the outcome of games in the March Madness Tournament. To make a long story short, I bought a Yaxel Lendeborg Michigan jersey later that day. My second bracket, with picks originating solely from the ML model, was named:

  Eric’s Evil Eye.


This article will describe how, although your human eyes may be deceived sometimes, the proof of success lies in the numbers, and a careful coding approach can lead to some strongly predictive performances.

My Unique Data Approach

Leading into the tournament, an idea kept banging around my head to train a machine learning model solely on college basketball teams’ relative strengths, instead of just their raw counting numbers. College basketball is a unique realm where stylistic matchup hunting and exposing relative weaknesses seem to matter so much in high pressure games that can be swung in just a few runs.

In fact, seeking relative advantages is important at any level of basketball. Even from a young age, a player will hear a coach say “he can’t dribble with his left so send him that way,” or, “she can’t shoot from 3 so sag off and prioritize protecting the paint.”

A great example of this stylistic game determinism is shown in the Cincinnati vs Kansas matchup from February 21st, 2026. Unranked Cincy took down the #8 Jayhawks (who were favored at -520 by DraftKings moneyline1) in what ended up being a dominant style late game after 12 lead changes through the first 30 minutes. Kansas, usually a top-ranked, assertive rebounding team was completely outclassed on the boards, losing the rebound battle 3-13 in the last 10.5 minutes of game time. The offensive boards nabbed by Cincy lead to kick out, wide-open threes, one of their very favorite looks this season. By February, Cincy was attempting 5.2 more 3’s per game, ranking 184 teams ahead of Kansas along this metric. This stylistic advantage paid off as Cincy shot 39% from downtown that game, making 8 more than Kansas (who shot 22%) and securing them a very respectable 84-68 win away from home2.

With this in mind, I knew the stats being fed into my March Madness model had to relate directly to how the two teams on the court stacked up against each other.

My hypothesis was that game outcomes could be predicted if the numbers revealed a team’s strong relative advantage against their opponent.

Data Challenges, Coding Process, and Description of the Model

Data Prep

I obtained the data for this project from two open-access Kaggle resources posted by Jonathan Pilafas3 and Nishaan Amin4. The former contains a wealth of regular season team-level statistics, collected and pooled from other sources like kenpom5, going back to the 2002 season. The latter contains each March Madness Tournament matchup, the seed numbers, and final game scores since 2008.

The main roadblock in carrying out the coding process for this project, as will sound familiar to experienced data scientists, was not actually in training the model itself, but in managing and uniting these two datasets. While one set contained team names like “Connecticut” and “Florida St.”, and the other containing “UConn” and “Florida State”, I knew I had to create some mapping system to marry these two. The planned 2 hours I set aside for this project turned into 10 due to specific, nuanced data challenges like these. In the end, I performed the mapping in Python (the coding language I used for all of this project) as meticulously and thoroughly as humanly possible, ensuring my final dataset could be trusted for analysis.

When I had the master historical dataset with each March Madness matchup, who won, and descriptive stats for each team, I then copied and reversed the pasted dataset, doubling it in size without changing any inherent qualities. Admittedly, this behavior sounds strange on first hearing. However, this is a commonly used tactic to cut down on potential biases the model may accidentally learn6. For example, while I may want the model to learn that the higher seeded team does in fact win a lot in March7, I don’t want it to start believing that the team listed first in the dataset wins a lot of the time just because it is listed first8.

Selecting the Features

But, which data should I care about for my study? I started with my own ball knowledge. To me, scoring, defense, rebounding, shooting efficiency, experience, coaching, and street cred (seed) are important factors when predicting the outcome of a basketball game. I performed investigatory research online and finalized a list of 19 team statistics, such as 3 point percentage, to be fed into my model9. These selected statistics will be called “features” to align with standard machine learning terminology.

The Random Forest Model

When my dataset was satisfactorily prepared, I trained my model using a machine learning tool called a “Random Forest Algorithm”. Given an input dataset, this algorithm creates a series of decision trees to make a prediction about new data. In my case, each decision tree looks at a subset of the data, deciding which feature values may be important for determining the outcome of a game, and casts an official vote as to which team will win. If this model were hypothetically applied to the Kansas vs Cincy game from February, for example, one branch of the tree may look at Kansas’s relative rebounding strength and defensive block percentage over Cincy, and cast a vote for Kansas to win as a result. Meanwhile, a few other trees may have looked at Cincy’s relative standout 3 point field goal rate, and sided with them instead. With many trees voting, the ensemble “forest” creates a final prediction via coded democracy. My model created 500 trees, so if 300 in the forest voted for Kansas, then the result would be a determined 60% probability of them winning:

\(\frac{300}{500} = 0.6\).

With that being done, all I had to do was input all of the first round matchups, and see what the model could cook up!

How Can the Model Be Trusted?

Arguably, the most important aspect of any ML algorithm is knowing that you can rely on its outputs. This model would have no advantages over a random coin toss, much less my own unshakeable eye test, if I didn’t know it’d have some strong predictive accuracy. Digging into the numbers, I segmented some of the master dataset away, calling it the test set, and reserving the bulk of the data to be the training set. I trained my model on the training set, and had it report back to me its predictive accuracy on the test set: 73.93% of the time it called the correct winner. This percentage is right at the forefront of top performing models designed with similar methods. For example, Shen et al. 201610 report a 71% accuracy from their RFA model in their study of the 2015 tournament. I knew the model could be improved yet, so I tuned it with a simple parameter-space search of hyperparameters to achieve the best possible model. This approach boosted my test-set prediction accuracy to 74.76%. Another important check includes the probability distribution plot, which shows how often a confidence interval was assigned to a game outcome. If the model assigns something near a 50% confidence interval to every game outcome, then you may as well save yourself the time and repeatedly flip a coin to fill out your bracket. On the other hand, if the model is close to 100% confident in every pick, you know it can’t be trusted because March Madness games are inherently chaotic, and many come down to last-second shots, or unpredictable human factors. Fig. 1 shows a simple visualization of the probability distribution of first round matchups in the 2026 tournament after one roll of the model. That most confidence levels fall in the 60-80% range is a great sign that this model is well-calibrated.

Results and Implications

Now to the fun part! How did the model perform in this year’s tournament, what spicy picks did it call, and how badly would it have dominated my family’s bracket pool?

Most Confident Predictions

My model was correctly the most confident that the following outcomes would occur:

  • Kansas beats California Baptist — 82.53%
  • Nebraska beats Troy — 80.11%
  • UCLA beats UCF — 78.42%

Games the Model Thought Could Go Either Way

  • <li>Georgia beats Saint Louis — 51.34%11</li>%
  • Saint John’s beats Northern Iowa — 58.69% (correct)
  • Ohio State beats TCU — 59.38% (correct)

The Model’s Upsets

The model predicted three upsets in the first round, all of which came true:

  • Iowa beats Clemson — 68.83%
  • VCU beats UNC — 60.08%
  • Utah State beats Villanova — 61.39%

The Model’s Worst Misses

  • High Point won against Wisconsin — 24.64%
  • Texas A&M won against Saint Mary’s — 36.83%
  • Texas won against BYU — 26.64%

The Final Score

In total, Eric’s Evil Eye correctly predicted 50/63 (79.3%)12 possible picks in the bracket, allowing it to rise to the 99.4th percentile of all brackets made on ESPN this year. The model had three of the correct Final Four members: Illinois, Arizona, and Michigan. The remaining member was Duke, who lost in a stunning, improbable fashion to UConn, although I could have told you Duke would be upset earlier than expected before coding a single thing. Investigating what made the model tick, I had it report which features it concluded to be the most important ones for determining the winner of a given game. As shown in Fig. 2, the three most important determining factors of what makes teams win in March are: kenpom adjusted offensive efficiency, kenpom adjusted defensive efficiency, and seed number13. Apparently not as important to the model are the active coaching length index, 3 point field goal attempt rate, and opponent block percentage. Therefore, this model confirms prior studies quoting kenpom statistics as the quick and simple gold standard for predictive accuracy in March14</sup>, and confirms my mom’s strategy of straying away from upsets.

Final Conclusion

For any fan of basketball, March Madness is the epitome of emotional rush. I experienced such a moment on April 4th, 2026, as the champion fighters of Eric’s Golden Mean and Eric’s Evil Eye faced off in a brutally anticipated Final Four game: Arizona versus Michigan. I went into this experiment hoping that basketball is not just an analytical game when it matters the most– that Arizona would prevail because I saw them dominate all regular season with my own eyes, and that heart wins over whatever the heck a forest algorithm is. That being said, when Michigan thumped Arizona essentially from the start, getting out to a 10-1 lead in the first three minutes, I couldn’t help but feel a deep sense of gratification and gratitude for the effort I put in on my code. Eric’s Golden Mean plummeted in my family’s bracket pool standings, yet I could hardly be seen without my Yaxel Lendeborg jersey from then on. In a single game elimination basketball tournament with 68 teams15, truly anything can happen. This project reminds me that you can create a nice image in your head of exactly how a game, or tournament, will play out, yet your one scenario will, statistically speaking, be out-maneuvered by intelligence propagated on years of historical data. Watching Yaxel literally put BTA in celebration with a NCAA Championship hat on his head, I leave feeling inspired to continue coding projects which highlight the heart that Michigan was not-so-secretly showing all year long. Next year, I’ll make sure my bracket is aligned in my newfound ideals:

  **Eric's Golden Eye.**

Footnotes

  1. This corresponds to about an 83.9% implied probability, for those not familiar with American betting odds. ↩
  2. Winning in Allen Fieldhouse is not easily done. The Jayhawks have won nearly 87% of their home games there historically. ↩
  3. Jonathan Pilafas, March Madness Historical DataSet (2002 to 2026), Kaggle. ↩
  4. Nishaan Amin, March Madness Data, Kaggle. ↩
  5. KenPom. ↩
  6. Eg. Romanov et al. (2023). ScienceDirect. ↩
  7. Higher seeds won 71.42% (797/1116) of March Madness games from the 2008–2026 Tournaments. ↩
  8. Higher seeds are typically listed first in the first round matchups due to how the bracket is laid out—which is purely an organizational thing and has nothing to do with the actual basketball being played on the court. ↩
  9. Please see the “Features Description” Page to better understand each feature and why they were selected in this study. ↩
  10. Shen et al. (2016). Conscientia Beam. ↩
  11. SLU won this game. In fact, when filling out the bracket for this model, randomly on the time I ran it, it correctly favored SLU winning this matchup. ↩
  12. A slightly higher percentage here than what was reported in the testing section just means that the model was a bit lucky this year! ↩
  13. Remember, all of these metrics are fed into the model as relative differences in each stat. ↩
  14. Power Ranking All 68 March Madness Teams Using KenPom , Bleacher Nation, March 20, 2025. ↩
  15. Now 76 teams starting next year! NCAA, “NCAA reveals new 76-team bracket for DI men's and women's basketball championships.” ↩

Figures & Plots

Figure 1 — Probability Distribution

The Probability Distribution histogram of First Round Matchups after one roll of the Random Forest Algorithm I designed for the March Madness 2026 Tournament. The logo for the higher seed in a given matchup is shown on the plot at a location corresponding to the likelihood they win their first round matchup.

Figure 2 — Feature Importance

The Normalized Feature Importances, as reported by the model via scikit-learn’s feature_importances_. Seemingly, kenpom stats and seed number matter a lot, although, surprisingly, experience, 3 point attempt rate, and active coaching length matter less as predictive metrics for March Madness game outcomes.

Figure 3 — Model Calibration

Top: Calibration curve of the Random Forest Algorithm on the historical test set. The blue curve shows the model’s predicted win probabilities on the x-axis compared to the true observed outcomes on the y, while the orange diagonal represents a perfectly calibrated model. Bottom: Distribution of predicted game win probabilities on the test set. Most predictions fall within the 60–80% confidence range, suggesting the model makes informed predictions without being unrealistically certain.

Figure 4 — Individual game Predictions

Running my model on single game outcomes produces the results shown. This approach yielded a 79.03% success rate. Unfortunately, the LIU Brooklyn Sharks were not represented in the dataset so no prediction was created for this outcome.

Figure 5 — Final Bracket Results

The final bracket with game outcomes is shown. This bracket was mostly successful, finishing in the 99.4th percentile of brackets on ESPN and correctly picking the Michigan Wolverines as this year’s March Madness champions.

Feature Descriptions

All statistics listed below were obtained from Jonathan Pilafas’s Kaggle page, “March Madness Historical DataSet (2002 to 2026)” on March 17th, 2026. Therefore, stats in the 2026 season correspond to regular season stats only. Unless otherwise specified, all stats reported here are team-level stats, counted by all player contributions on the team within the given season. The original data source for all stats listed below is kenpom.com.

Adjusted Offensive Efficiency — AdjO

Offensive Efficiency measures the points a team scores per 100 possessions across the season. This stat has been adjusted by Pomeroy to adjust for the strength of opponents played in the season so that AdjO can be compared directly between all D1 teams.

Adjusted Defensive Efficiency — AdjD

Defensive Efficiency measures the points a team concedes per 100 possessions across the season. This stat has been adjusted by Pomeroy to adjust for the strength of opponents played in the season so that AdjD can be compared directly between all D1 teams.

Adjusted Tempo — AdjTempo

Tempo measures the possessions a team has per 40 minutes across the season. This stat has been adjusted by Pomeroy to adjust for the tempo of opponents played in the season so that AdjD can be compared directly between all D1 teams.

FG2Pct

The percentage of field goals a team successfully makes from within the arc, equivalent to a 2-point bucket.

FG3Pct

The percentage of field goals made from outside the arc, equivalent to a 3-point bucket.

FTPct

The percentage of free throws a team makes.

BlockPct

The percentage of opposing team 2-point field goal attempts that are blocked by the pertinent team.

StlRate

The percentage of opponent possessions that end in a steal by the pertinent team.

FG3Rate

The percentage of possessions during which a team attempts a 3 point field goal.

OppFG2Pct

The percentage of 2 point field goals opponents make against a team.

OppFG3Pct

The percentage of 3 point field goals opponents make against a team.

OppBlockPct

The percentage of possessions where a team is blocked by the opposition on a shot attempt.

OppStlRate

The percentage of possessions where a team has the ball stolen by the opposition.

OppFG3Rate

The percentage of 3 point field goals that are made by opposing teams against the pertinent team.

Experience

An estimate of the average number of Division I basketball seasons played by a roster, weighted by minutes played.

Bench

An estimate of the percentage of a team’s total minutes played by non-starters, reflecting roster depth and rotation usage.

Active Coaching Length Index

A measure of the tenure and continuity of the current head coach of a team, indexed relative to other head coaches.

Seed

The assigned NCAA Tournament Seed for a team going into March Madness. Lower numbered seeds reflect stronger teams as determined by the March Madness Selection Committee and they range 1-16.

ORPct

Offensive Rebound Percentage, representing the percentage of available offensive rebounds a team secures after missed shots.

Data Sources

  • Jonathan Pilafas — March Madness Historical DataSet (2002 to 2026)
  • Nishaan Amin — March Madness Data
  • KenPom — regular-season team statistics
  • Shen et al. (2016) — Random Forest March Madness prediction methodology

entry.title: Google Gemini updates: Flash 1.5, Gemma 2 and Project Astra

link.title: Google Gemini updates: Flash 1.5, Gemma 2 and Project Astra

entry.content:
Gemini breaks new ground with a faster model, longer context, AI agents and moreLearn more:Learn more:Learn more:Models & ResearchProductsInfrastructure & cloudTechnology Learn more: ProductsPlatformsDevices Learn more: Outreach & initiativesLeadershipInside Google Learn more: May 14, 2024 We’re introducing a series of updates across the Gemini family of models, including the new 1.5 Flash, our lightweight model for speed and efficiency, and Project Astra, our vision for the future of AI assistants. Demis HassabisCEO of Google DeepMind, on behalf of the Gemini teamIn December, we launched our first natively multimodal model Gemini 1.0 in three sizes: Ultra, Pro and Nano. Just a few months later we released 1.5 Pro, with enhanced performance and a breakthrough long context window of 1 million tokens.Developers and enterprise customers have been putting 1.5 Pro to use in incredible ways and finding its long context window, multimodal reasoning capabilities and impressive overall performance incredibly useful.We know from user feedback that some applications need lower latency and a lower cost to serve. This inspired us to keep innovating, so today, we’re introducing Gemini 1.5 Flash: a model that’s lighter-weight than 1.5 Pro, and designed to be fast and efficient to serve at scale.Both 1.5 Pro and 1.5 Flash are available in public preview with a 1 million token context window in Google AI Studio and Vertex AI. And now, 1.5 Pro is also available with a 2 million token context window via waitlist to developers using the API and to Google Cloud customers.We’re also introducing updates across the Gemini family of models, announcing our next generation of open models, Gemma 2, and sharing progress on the future of AI assistants, with Project Astra.Context lengths of leading foundation models compared with Gemini 1.5’s 2 million token capability1.5 Flash is the newest addition to the Gemini model family and the fastest Gemini model served in the API. It’s optimized for high-volume, high-frequency tasks at scale, is more cost-efficient to serve and features our breakthrough long context window.While it’s a lighter weight model than 1.5 Pro, it’s highly capable of multimodal reasoning across vast amounts of information and delivers impressive quality for its size.The new Gemini 1.5 Flash model is optimized for speed and efficiency, is highly capable of multimodal reasoning and features our breakthrough long context window.1.5 Flash excels at summarization, chat applications, image and video captioning, data extraction from long documents and tables, and more. This is because it’s been trained by 1.5 Pro through a process called “distillation,” where the most essential knowledge and skills from a larger model are transferred to a smaller, more efficient model.Read more about 1.5 Flash in our updated Gemini 1.5 technical report, on the Gemini technology page, and learn about 1.5 Flash’s availability and pricing.Over the last few months, we’ve significantly improved 1.5 Pro, our best model for general performance across a wide range of tasks.Beyond extending its context window to 2 million tokens, we’ve enhanced its code generation, logical reasoning and planning, multi-turn conversation, and audio and image understanding through data and algorithmic advances. We see strong improvements on public and internal benchmarks for each of these tasks.1.5 Pro can now follow increasingly complex and nuanced instructions, including ones that specify product-level behavior involving role, format and style. We’ve improved control over the model’s responses for specific use cases, like crafting the persona and response style of a chat agent or automating workflows through multiple function calls. And we’ve enabled users to steer model behavior by setting system instructions.We added audio understanding in the Gemini API and Google AI Studio, so 1.5 Pro can now reason across image and audio for videos uploaded in Google AI Studio. And we’re now integrating 1.5 Pro into Google products, including Gemini Advanced and in Workspace apps.Read more about 1.5 Pro in our updated Gemini 1.5 technical report and on the Gemini technology page.Gemini Nano is expanding beyond text-only inputs to include images as well. Starting with Pixel, applications using Gemini Nano with Multimodality will be able to understand the world the way people do — not just through text, but also through sight, sound and spoken language.Read more about Gemini 1.0 Nano on Android.Today, we’re also sharing a series of updates to Gemma, our family of open models built from the same research and technology used to create the Gemini models.We’re announcing Gemma 2, our next generation of open models for responsible AI innovation. Gemma 2 has a new architecture designed for breakthrough performance and efficiency, and will be available in new sizes.The Gemma family is also expanding with PaliGemma, our first vision-language model inspired by PaLI-3. And we’ve upgraded our Responsible Generative AI Toolkit with LLM Comparator for evaluating the quality of model responses.Read more on the Developer blog.As part of Google DeepMind’s mission to build AI responsibly to benefit humanity, we’ve always wanted to develop universal AI agents that can be helpful in everyday life. That’s why today, we’re sharing our progress in building the future of AI assistants with Project Astra (advanced seeing and talking responsive agent).To be truly useful, an agent needs to understand and respond to the complex and dynamic world just like people do — and take in and remember what it sees and hears to understand context and take action. It also needs to be proactive, teachable and personal, so users can talk to it naturally and without lag or delay.While we’ve made incredible progress developing AI systems that can understand multimodal information, getting response time down to something conversational is a difficult engineering challenge. Over the past few years, we’ve been working to improve how our models perceive, reason and converse to make the pace and quality of interaction feel more natural.Building on Gemini, we’ve developed prototype agents that can process information faster by continuously encoding video frames, combining the video and speech input into a timeline of events, and caching this information for efficient recall.By leveraging our leading speech models, we also enhanced how they sound, giving the agents a wider range of intonations. These agents can better understand the context they’re being used in, and respond quickly, in conversation.With technology like this, it’s easy to envision a future where people could have an expert AI assistant by their side, through a phone or glasses. And some of these capabilities are coming to Google products, like the Gemini app and web experience, later this year.We’ve made incredible progress so far with our family of Gemini models, and we’re always striving to advance the state-of-the-art even further. By investing in a relentless production line of innovation, we’re able to explore new ideas at the frontier, while also unlocking the possibility of new and exciting Gemini use cases.Learn more about Gemini and its capabilities.Collection Sign up for our newsletters with product updates, event information, special offers, and more. Done. Just one step more. Check your inbox to confirm your subscription.

You can also subscribe with a different email address.

Content 2

{% endtab %}

{% endtabs %}

With this you can generate visualizations like:

  • php

  • ruby 
  • var_dump('hello');

  • console.log("hello");

  • pputs 'hello'

Another example

  • yaml
  • json 
  • hello:
  - "whatsup"
  - "hi"

  • {
  "hello": ["whatsup", "hi"]
}

Tabs for something else

  • text
  • quote
  • list

  • Regular text

  • A quote

  • Hipster list

    • brunch
    • fixie
    • raybans

entry.title: a post with pseudo code
entry.content:
This is an example post with some pseudo code rendered by pseudocode. The example presented here is the same as the one in the pseudocode.js documentation, with only one simple but important change: everytime you would use $, you should use $$ instead. Also, note that the pseudocode key in the front matter is set to true to enable the rendering of pseudo code. As an example, using this code:

```pseudocode
% This quicksort algorithm is extracted from Chapter 7, Introduction to Algorithms (3rd edition)
\begin{algorithm}
\caption{Quicksort}
\begin{algorithmic}
\PROCEDURE{Quicksort}{$$A, p, r$$}
    \IF{$$p < r$$}
        \STATE $$q = $$ \CALL{Partition}{$$A, p, r$$}
        \STATE \CALL{Quicksort}{$$A, p, q - 1$$}
        \STATE \CALL{Quicksort}{$$A, q + 1, r$$}
    \ENDIF
\ENDPROCEDURE
\PROCEDURE{Partition}{$$A, p, r$$}
    \STATE $$x = A[r]$$
    \STATE $$i = p - 1$$
    \FOR{$$j = p$$ \TO $$r - 1$$}
        \IF{$$A[j] < x$$}
            \STATE $$i = i + 1$$
            \STATE exchange
            $$A[i]$$ with $$A[j]$$
        \ENDIF
        \STATE exchange $$A[i]$$ with $$A[r]$$
    \ENDFOR
\ENDPROCEDURE
\end{algorithmic}
\end{algorithm}
```

Generates:

    \ENDIF
\ENDPROCEDURE

entry.title: a post with code diff
entry.content:
You can display diff code by using the regular markdown syntax:

```diff
diff --git a/sample.js b/sample.js
index 0000001..0ddf2ba
--- a/sample.js
+++ b/sample.js
@@ -1 +1 @@
-console.log("Hello World!")
+console.log("Hello from Diff2Html!")
```

Which generates:

diff --git a/sample.js b/sample.js
index 0000001..0ddf2ba
--- a/sample.js
+++ b/sample.js
@@ -1 +1 @@
-console.log("Hello World!")
+console.log("Hello from Diff2Html!")

But this is difficult to read, specially if you have a large diff. You can use diff2html to display a more readable version of the diff. For this, just use diff2html instead of diff for the code block language:

```diff2html
diff --git a/sample.js b/sample.js
index 0000001..0ddf2ba
--- a/sample.js
+++ b/sample.js
@@ -1 +1 @@
-console.log("Hello World!")
+console.log("Hello from Diff2Html!")
```

If we use a longer example, for example this commit from diff2html, it will generate the following output:

   - `synchronisedScroll`: scroll both panes in side-by-side mode: `true` or `false`, default is `false`
   - `matchWordsThreshold`: similarity threshold for word matching, default is 0.25
   - `matchingMaxComparisons`: perform at most this much comparisons for line matching a block of changes, default is `2500`
+  - `templates`: object with previously compiled templates to replace parts of the html

   function HoganJsUtils(configuration) {
     this.config = configuration || {};
     extraTemplates = this.config.templates || {};
+
+    var rawTemplates = this.config.rawTemplates || {};
+    for (var templateName in rawTemplates) {
+      if (rawTemplates.hasOwnProperty(templateName)) {
+        if (!extraTemplates[templateName]) extraTemplates[templateName] = this.compile(rawTemplates[templateName]);

+    }
   }

entry.title: a post with vega lite
entry.content:
This is an example post with some vega lite code.

```vega_lite
{
  "$schema": "https://vega.github.io/schema/vega-lite/v5.json",
  "description": "A dot plot showing each movie in the database, and the difference from the average movie rating. The display is sorted by year to visualize everything in sequential order. The graph is for all Movies before 2019.",
  "data": {
    "url": "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/vega/vega/main/docs/data/movies.json"
  },
  "transform": [
    {"filter": "datum['IMDB Rating'] != null"},
    {"filter": {"timeUnit": "year", "field": "Release Date", "range": [null, 2019]}},
    {
      "joinaggregate": [{
        "op": "mean",
        "field": "IMDB Rating",
        "as": "AverageRating"
      }]
    },
    {
      "calculate": "datum['IMDB Rating'] - datum.AverageRating",
      "as": "RatingDelta"
    }
  ],
  "mark": "point",
  "encoding": {
    "x": {
      "field": "Release Date",
      "type": "temporal"
    },
    "y": {
      "field": "RatingDelta",
      "type": "quantitative",
      "title": "Rating Delta"
    },
    "color": {
      "field": "RatingDelta",
      "type": "quantitative",
      "scale": {"domainMid": 0},
      "title": "Rating Delta"
    }
  }
}
```

Which generates:

{
  "$schema": "https://vega.github.io/schema/vega-lite/v5.json",
  "description": "A dot plot showing each movie in the database, and the difference from the average movie rating. The display is sorted by year to visualize everything in sequential order. The graph is for all Movies before 2019.",
  "data": {
    "url": "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/vega/vega/main/docs/data/movies.json"
  },
  "transform": [
    {"filter": "datum['IMDB Rating'] != null"},
    {"filter": {"timeUnit": "year", "field": "Release Date", "range": [null, 2019]}},
    {
      "joinaggregate": [{
        "op": "mean",
        "field": "IMDB Rating",
        "as": "AverageRating"
      }]
    },
    {
      "calculate": "datum['IMDB Rating'] - datum.AverageRating",
      "as": "RatingDelta"
    }
  ],
  "mark": "point",
  "encoding": {
    "x": {
      "field": "Release Date",
      "type": "temporal"
    },
    "y": {
      "field": "RatingDelta",
      "type": "quantitative",
      "title": "Rating Delta"
    },
    "color": {
      "field": "RatingDelta",
      "type": "quantitative",
      "scale": {"domainMid": 0},
      "title": "Rating Delta"
    }
  }
}

This plot supports both light and dark themes.
